name: Sternocleidomastoid
etymology: From Greek sternon ‘chest/breastbone’ + kleis, kleidos ‘key’ (the clavicle) + mastoeidēs ‘breast-shaped’ (mastos ‘breast’ + eidos ‘form’). So it means ‘the sternum-and-clavicle-to-mastoid muscle’ — named exactly for its three attachments.
origin: Sternal head: anterior surface of manubrium; clavicular head: superior surface of medial third of clavicle
insertion: Lateral surface of mastoid process and lateral half of superior nuchal line
actions: Head/neck rotation to the opposite side (unilateral)
Accessory inspiration (elevates sternum when head is fixed)
innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioception from C2–C3
tip: Tight, overactive SCM goes with forward-head posture; to stretch the right SCM, laterally flex left and rotate the head right with slight extension.

name: Platysma
etymology: From Greek platysma ‘a flat plate’, from platys ‘broad, flat’. So it means ‘the flat sheet’ — a thin, broad sheet of muscle lying in the skin of the neck.
origin: Superficial fascia over upper pectoralis major and deltoid
insertion: Inferior border of mandible, skin of lower face and angle of mouth (modiolus)
actions: Depresses the angle of the mouth and lower lip
Tenses the skin of the neck (grimace)
tip: A facial-expression muscle in the neck — so it is supplied by CN VII, not a cervical spinal nerve.

name: Anterior scalene
etymology: From Greek skalēnos ‘uneven, unequal’ (as in a scalene triangle with unequal sides) + Latin anterior ‘front’. So it means ‘the front uneven muscle’ — the scalenes are three unequal muscles that together form a lopsided triangle on the side of the neck.
origin: Anterior tubercles of transverse processes of C3–C6
insertion: Scalene tubercle on inner border of 1st rib
actions: Slight cervical rotation to the opposite side
tip: Thoracic outlet: the brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between anterior and middle scalenes (subclavian vein passes in front), so a tight anterior scalene can compress them; the phrenic nerve lies on its front.

name: Middle scalene
etymology: From Greek skalēnos ‘uneven, unequal’ + Latin medius ‘middle’. So it means ‘the middle uneven muscle’ — the middle and largest of the three scalenes.
origin: Posterior tubercles of transverse processes of C2–C7 (often also atlas)
insertion: Superior surface of 1st rib, behind the groove for the subclavian artery
tip: Forms the back wall of the interscalene triangle — part of the scalene-related thoracic outlet syndrome picture with the anterior scalene.

name: Posterior scalene
etymology: From Greek skalēnos ‘uneven, unequal’ + Latin posterior ‘behind’. So it means ‘the back uneven muscle’ — the smallest, most posterior scalene.
origin: Posterior tubercles of transverse processes of C4–C6
insertion: External surface of 2nd rib
tip: The only scalene that reaches the 2nd rib — scalenes overwork as breathing muscles in apical/chest breathers.

name: Longus colli
etymology: From Latin longus ‘long’ + colli ‘of the neck’ (collum). So it means ‘the long muscle of the neck’ — it runs a long way down the front of the cervical and upper thoracic spine.
origin: Bodies of T1–T3 and C5–C7; anterior tubercles of transverse processes of C3–C5
insertion: Anterior tubercle of atlas; bodies of C2–C4; anterior tubercles of transverse processes of C5–C6
actions: Slight cervical rotation to the opposite side
tip: A key deep neck flexor — weak in forward-head posture and after whiplash; train it with chin tucks / the craniocervical flexion test.

name: Longus capitis
etymology: From Latin longus ‘long’ + capitis ‘of the head’ (caput). So it means ‘the long muscle of the head’ — a long prevertebral muscle running from the neck up to the skull.
origin: Anterior tubercles of transverse processes of C3–C6
insertion: Basilar part of occipital bone
tip: Works with longus colli as a deep neck flexor; the ‘nod’ in a chin tuck comes from it.

name: Rectus capitis anterior
etymology: From Latin rectus ‘straight’ + capitis ‘of the head’ + anterior ‘front’. So it means ‘the straight front muscle of the head’ — a short, straight muscle in front of the atlanto-occipital joint.
origin: Anterior surface of lateral mass of atlas (C1)
insertion: Basilar part of occipital bone, in front of the occipital condyle
actions: Head flexion at the atlanto-occipital joint
tip: Tiny deep craniocervical flexor — the anterior counterpart of the suboccipitals.

name: Rectus capitis lateralis
etymology: From Latin rectus ‘straight’ + capitis ‘of the head’ + lateralis ‘of the side’. So it means ‘the straight side muscle of the head’ — a short vertical muscle on the side of the atlanto-occipital joint.
origin: Superior surface of transverse process of atlas (C1)
insertion: Jugular process of occipital bone
tip: Considered the upper-cervical equivalent of a posterior intertransverse muscle.

name: Rectus capitis posterior major
etymology: From Latin rectus ‘straight’ + capitis ‘of the head’ + posterior ‘behind’ + major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger straight back muscle of the head’ — the bigger of the two straight suboccipital muscles.
origin: Spinous process of axis (C2)
insertion: Lateral part of inferior nuchal line of occipital bone
actions: Head rotation to the same side
tip: Suboccipitals stay shortened in forward-head posture (chin poked, upper neck extended) and are a classic source of cervicogenic headache.

name: Rectus capitis posterior minor
etymology: From Latin rectus ‘straight’ + capitis ‘of the head’ + posterior ‘behind’ + minor ‘smaller’. So it means ‘the smaller straight back muscle of the head’ — the smaller, more medial straight suboccipital.
origin: Posterior tubercle of atlas (C1)
insertion: Medial part of inferior nuchal line of occipital bone
tip: Has a connective-tissue ‘myodural bridge’ to the dura mater — linked to headaches in forward-head posture.

name: Obliquus capitis superior
etymology: From Latin obliquus ‘slanting’ + capitis ‘of the head’ + superior ‘upper’. So it means ‘the upper slanting muscle of the head’ — its fibres slant up and back from atlas to skull.
origin: Transverse process of atlas (C1)
insertion: Occipital bone between superior and inferior nuchal lines (lateral part)
tip: Forms the upper-lateral side of the suboccipital triangle (vertebral artery and C1 run in its floor).

name: Obliquus capitis inferior
etymology: From Latin obliquus ‘slanting’ + capitis ‘of the head’ + inferior ‘lower’. So it means ‘the lower slanting muscle of the head’ — even though, oddly, it never touches the skull.
origin: Spinous process of axis (C2)
insertion: Transverse process of atlas (C1)
actions: Head rotation to the same side (at the atlanto-axial joint)
tip: The only ‘capitis’ muscle with no skull attachment — it turns C1 (and the head) on C2.

name: Digastric
etymology: From Greek di- ‘two’ + gastēr ‘belly’. So it means ‘two-bellied’ — anterior and posterior bellies joined by an intermediate tendon.
origin: Anterior belly: digastric fossa of mandible; posterior belly: mastoid notch of temporal bone
insertion: Intermediate tendon, held to body and greater horn of hyoid by a fibrous sling
actions: Depresses mandible (mouth opening, esp. against resistance)
innervation: Anterior belly: nerve to mylohyoid (CN V3); posterior belly: facial nerve (CN VII)
tip: Two bellies, two embryonic origins, two nerves — a favourite exam question.

name: Stylohyoid
etymology: From Greek stylos ‘pillar, stake’ (the styloid process) + hyoeidēs ‘U-shaped’ (letter upsilon + eidos ‘form’, the hyoid bone). So it means ‘the styloid-to-hyoid muscle’.
origin: Styloid process of temporal bone
insertion: Body of hyoid (near greater horn); split around the digastric tendon
tip: Its insertion splits to let the digastric’s intermediate tendon pass through.

name: Mylohyoid
etymology: From Greek mylē ‘mill’ (referring to the molar or ‘grinding’ teeth) + hyoeidēs ‘U-shaped’ (hyoid). So it means ‘the molar-region-to-hyoid muscle’ — it arises from the mylohyoid line beneath the molars.
origin: Mylohyoid line of mandible
insertion: Median raphe and body of hyoid
actions: Elevates hyoid and floor of mouth (swallowing)
tip: Forms the muscular floor of the mouth (‘oral diaphragm’).

name: Geniohyoid
etymology: From Greek geneion ‘chin’ + hyoeidēs ‘U-shaped’ (hyoid). So it means ‘the chin-to-hyoid muscle’.
origin: Inferior mental spine (genial tubercle) of mandible
insertion: Body of hyoid
actions: Depresses mandible when hyoid is fixed
innervation: C1 fibres carried by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
tip: Sits just above the mylohyoid — supplied by C1 ‘hitch-hiking’ on CN XII.

name: Omohyoid
etymology: From Greek ōmos ‘shoulder’ + hyoeidēs ‘U-shaped’ (hyoid). So it means ‘the shoulder-to-hyoid muscle’ — it runs from the scapula to the hyoid.
origin: Inferior belly: superior border of scapula near suprascapular notch
insertion: Superior belly: inferior border of body of hyoid (intermediate tendon tethered to clavicle by a fascial sling)
tip: Two bellies with an intermediate tendon — a landmark dividing the anterior and posterior triangles of the neck.

name: Sternohyoid
etymology: From Greek sternon ‘chest, breastbone’ + hyoeidēs ‘U-shaped’ (hyoid). So it means ‘the sternum-to-hyoid muscle’.
origin: Posterior surface of manubrium and medial end of clavicle
insertion: Body of hyoid
tip: Superficial ‘strap muscle’ of the infrahyoid group.

name: Sternothyroid
etymology: From Greek sternon ‘breastbone’ + thyreoeidēs ‘shield-shaped’ (thyreos ‘oblong shield’, the thyroid cartilage). So it means ‘the sternum-to-thyroid-cartilage muscle’.
origin: Posterior surface of manubrium
insertion: Oblique line of thyroid cartilage
tip: Lies deep to sternohyoid; continues upward as thyrohyoid.

name: Thyrohyoid
etymology: From Greek thyreoeidēs ‘shield-shaped’ (thyroid cartilage) + hyoeidēs ‘U-shaped’ (hyoid). So it means ‘the thyroid-cartilage-to-hyoid muscle’.
origin: Oblique line of thyroid cartilage
insertion: Inferior border of body and greater horn of hyoid
actions: Elevates larynx when hyoid is fixed
innervation: C1 fibres carried by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
tip: The one infrahyoid not supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop itself.

name: Temporalis
etymology: From Latin tempora ‘the temples’ (plural of tempus, which also means ‘time’ — probably because grey hair first shows there). So it means ‘the muscle of the temple’.
origin: Floor of temporal fossa and deep surface of temporal fascia
insertion: Coronoid process and anterior border of ramus of mandible
tip: Palpate at the temple while clenching; trigger points here commonly refer pain as temporal headache and with jaw clenching/bruxism.

name: Masseter
etymology: From Greek masētēr ‘chewer’ (from masasthai ‘to chew’). So it means ‘the chewer’ — the main muscle you feel bulge when chewing.
origin: Superficial part: zygomatic process of maxilla and anterior two-thirds of zygomatic arch; deep part: posterior third and medial surface of zygomatic arch
insertion: Lateral surface of ramus and angle of mandible (deep part higher, up to coronoid process)
tip: Strongest muscle for its size; often tender in bruxism and TMJ dysfunction — palpate at the angle of the jaw while clenching.

name: Medial pterygoid
etymology: From Greek pteryx ‘wing’ + eidos ‘form’ (the wing-like pterygoid plates of the sphenoid) + Latin medialis ‘toward the middle’. So it means ‘the inner wing-shaped-plate muscle’.
origin: Deep head: medial surface of lateral pterygoid plate (and pyramidal process of palatine); superficial head: tuberosity of maxilla
insertion: Medial surface of ramus near angle of mandible
tip: Forms a ‘sling’ around the angle of the mandible with the masseter.

name: Lateral pterygoid
parts: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
etymology: From Greek pteryx ‘wing’ + eidos ‘form’ (pterygoid plates of the sphenoid) + Latin lateralis ‘of the side’. So it means ‘the outer wing-shaped-plate muscle’.
origin: Superior head: infratemporal surface and crest of greater wing of sphenoid; inferior head: lateral surface of lateral pterygoid plate
insertion: Pterygoid fovea on neck of mandibular condyle; superior head also into TMJ articular disc and capsule
actions: Mandible depression / mouth opening (inferior head pulls condyle forward)
Stabilises TMJ disc during closing (superior head)
tip: Key TMJ muscle: it attaches to the articular disc, so its dysfunction is linked to disc displacement, clicking and jaw deviation on opening.

name: Frontalis
etymology: From Latin frons, frontis ‘forehead’. So it means ‘the forehead muscle’.
origin: Epicranial aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica)
insertion: Skin and fascia of eyebrows and forehead
tip: Ask the patient to raise the eyebrows to test the temporal branch of CN VII (spared on the forehead in a central/stroke facial palsy, lost in Bell’s palsy).

name: Occipitalis
etymology: From Latin occiput ‘back of the head’ (ob ‘against, behind’ + caput ‘head’). So it means ‘the back-of-the-head muscle’.
origin: Lateral two-thirds of superior nuchal line and mastoid process
insertion: Epicranial aponeurosis
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), posterior auricular branch
tip: Paired with frontalis through the galea as one ‘occipitofrontalis’ unit.

name: Temporoparietalis
etymology: From Latin tempora ‘temples’ + paries, parietis ‘wall’ (the parietal bone). So it means ‘the temple-and-parietal muscle’ — a thin sheet over the side of the skull.
origin: Temporal fascia above and in front of the ear
insertion: Lateral border of epicranial aponeurosis
tip: A variable, thin scalp muscle — often absent or blended with the auricular muscles.

name: Orbicularis oculi
etymology: From Latin orbiculus ‘small disc, little circle’ + oculi ‘of the eye’ (oculus). So it means ‘the little circular muscle of the eye’ — a sphincter ring around the eye.
origin: Nasal part of frontal bone, frontal process of maxilla, medial palpebral ligament (and lacrimal bone, lacrimal part)
insertion: Skin around the orbit; palpebral part to lateral palpebral raphe
actions: Forced, tight eyelid closure / squinting (orbital part)
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), temporal and zygomatic branches
tip: Inability to close the eye tightly is a hallmark of Bell’s palsy (CN VII).

name: Corrugator supercilii
etymology: From Latin corrugare ‘to wrinkle’ (com- + ruga ‘wrinkle’) + supercilii ‘of the eyebrow’ (supercilium). So it means ‘the eyebrow wrinkler’.
origin: Medial end of superciliary arch of frontal bone
insertion: Skin above the middle of the eyebrow
actions: Produces vertical frown lines between the brows
tip: The ‘worried frown’ muscle — a common target of cosmetic botulinum toxin.

name: Procerus
etymology: From Latin procerus ‘long, stretched out, tall’. So it means ‘the long (slender) muscle’ — probably for its elongated shape running up the bridge of the nose.
origin: Fascia over nasal bone and upper lateral nasal cartilage
insertion: Skin of lower forehead between the eyebrows
actions: Makes transverse wrinkles over the bridge of the nose
tip: Creates the horizontal ‘bunny line’ at the nose bridge when frowning or squinting into sun.

name: Nasalis
etymology: From Latin nasus ‘nose’. So it means ‘the nose muscle’.
origin: Maxilla lateral to the nose, above the incisor and canine teeth
insertion: Transverse part: aponeurosis over nasal bridge; alar part: alar cartilage
tip: Flaring nostrils (alar part) is a sign of increased work of breathing.

name: Depressor septi nasi
etymology: From Latin depressor ‘one that presses down’ + septi ‘of the partition’ (septum ‘fence, partition’) + nasi ‘of the nose’. So it means ‘the puller-down of the nasal septum’.
origin: Incisive fossa of maxilla
insertion: Mobile part of nasal septum and ala
tip: Its pull drops the nasal tip when smiling.

name: Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi
etymology: From Latin levator ‘lifter’ + labii superioris ‘of the upper lip’ + alaeque nasi ‘and of the wing of the nose’ (ala ‘wing’, -que ‘and’, nasus ‘nose’). So it means ‘the lifter of the upper lip and the wing of the nose’.
origin: Frontal process of maxilla
insertion: Alar cartilage of the nose and skin of upper lip
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), zygomatic and buccal branches
tip: Famous for having the longest muscle name — the ‘Elvis sneer’ muscle.

name: Levator labii superioris
etymology: From Latin levator ‘lifter’ + labii ‘of the lip’ (labium) + superioris ‘upper’. So it means ‘the lifter of the upper lip’.
origin: Infra-orbital margin of maxilla, above the infra-orbital foramen
insertion: Skin and muscle of the upper lip
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), zygomatic and buccal branches
tip: Lies between levator labii superioris alaeque nasi (medial) and zygomaticus minor (lateral).

name: Levator anguli oris
etymology: From Latin levator ‘lifter’ + anguli ‘of the corner’ (angulus) + oris ‘of the mouth’ (os). So it means ‘the lifter of the corner of the mouth’.
origin: Canine fossa of maxilla, below the infra-orbital foramen
insertion: Modiolus at the angle of the mouth
actions: Elevates the angle of the mouth
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), zygomatic and buccal branches
tip: Deep to levator labii superioris — helps produce a closed-lip smile.

name: Zygomaticus major
etymology: From Greek zygon ‘yoke’ (the zygomatic bone/arch joins face and skull like a yoke) + Latin major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger cheekbone muscle’.
origin: Lateral surface of zygomatic bone (posterior part)
insertion: Modiolus at the angle of the mouth
actions: Draws the angle of the mouth up and laterally (smiling)
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), zygomatic and buccal branches
tip: The main smiling muscle — ask the patient to smile to test lower CN VII.

name: Zygomaticus minor
etymology: From Greek zygon ‘yoke’ (zygomatic bone) + Latin minor ‘smaller’. So it means ‘the smaller cheekbone muscle’.
origin: Anterior surface of zygomatic bone
insertion: Lateral part of the upper lip
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), zygomatic and buccal branches
tip: Inserts into the lip, not the mouth corner — it lifts the lip to show the upper teeth.

name: Risorius
etymology: From Latin risus ‘laughter’ (ridere ‘to laugh’). So it means ‘the laughing muscle’.
origin: Parotid fascia and fascia over masseter
insertion: Modiolus at the angle of the mouth
actions: Retracts the angle of the mouth laterally (grin, grimace)
tip: Pulls the mouth corner straight sideways — more grimace than true smile.

name: Orbicularis oris
etymology: From Latin orbiculus ‘little circle’ + oris ‘of the mouth’ (os). So it means ‘the little circular muscle of the mouth’ — a sphincter around the lips.
origin: Maxilla and mandible near the midline, and fibres from surrounding facial muscles (esp. buccinator)
insertion: Skin and mucous membrane of the lips
actions: Protrudes and purses the lips (whistling, kissing)
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), buccal and marginal mandibular branches
tip: Test CN VII by asking the patient to puff the cheeks with lips sealed.

name: Depressor anguli oris
etymology: From Latin depressor ‘one that presses down’ + anguli ‘of the corner’ + oris ‘of the mouth’. So it means ‘the puller-down of the corner of the mouth’.
origin: Oblique line of mandible, below the canine and premolars
insertion: Modiolus at the angle of the mouth
actions: Depresses the angle of the mouth (frowning, sadness)
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), marginal mandibular branch
tip: Triangular in shape — the ‘sad face’ muscle.

name: Depressor labii inferioris
etymology: From Latin depressor ‘one that presses down’ + labii ‘of the lip’ + inferioris ‘lower’. So it means ‘the puller-down of the lower lip’.
origin: Oblique line of mandible, between the symphysis and mental foramen (deep to depressor anguli oris)
insertion: Skin and mucosa of the lower lip
actions: Depresses the lower lip and draws it laterally
Everts the lower lip (pouting, showing lower teeth)
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), marginal mandibular branch
tip: Weakness gives an asymmetric lower lip when showing the teeth — a sign of marginal mandibular nerve injury.

name: Mentalis
etymology: From Latin mentum ‘chin’. So it means ‘the chin muscle’.
origin: Incisive fossa of mandible
insertion: Skin of the chin
actions: Elevates and protrudes the lower lip (pouting, drinking)
Wrinkles the skin of the chin
innervation: Facial nerve (CN VII), marginal mandibular branch
tip: The ‘dimpled/golf-ball chin’ muscle when you push your lower lip up.

name: Buccinator
etymology: From Latin buccinator ‘trumpeter’, from buccina ‘trumpet’ (related to bucca ‘cheek’). So it means ‘the trumpeter’s muscle’ — it compresses the cheek to blow air out.
origin: Alveolar processes of maxilla and mandible opposite the molars, and pterygomandibular raphe
insertion: Angle of the mouth, blending into orbicularis oris
actions: Compresses the cheek against the teeth (keeps food between molars)
tip: Motor by CN VII — don’t confuse with the buccal nerve of CN V3, which is only sensory to the cheek.

name: Superior rectus
etymology: From Latin superior ‘upper’ + rectus ‘straight’. So it means ‘the upper straight muscle’ of the eye.
origin: Common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn)
insertion: Superior sclera, anterior to the equator of the eyeball
tip: Test in the H-pattern: look out (abduct) then up — elevation is purely superior rectus in abduction.

name: Inferior rectus
etymology: From Latin inferior ‘lower’ + rectus ‘straight’. So it means ‘the lower straight muscle’ of the eye.
origin: Common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn)
insertion: Inferior sclera, anterior to the equator of the eyeball
tip: Test in the H-pattern: look out (abduct) then down. Can be entrapped in an orbital floor ‘blow-out’ fracture.

name: Medial rectus
etymology: From Latin medialis ‘toward the middle’ + rectus ‘straight’. So it means ‘the inner straight muscle’ of the eye.
origin: Common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn)
insertion: Medial sclera, anterior to the equator of the eyeball
tip: Remember ‘LR6 SO4, the rest 3’ — medial rectus is CN III; with a CN III palsy the eye rests ‘down and out’.

name: Lateral rectus
etymology: From Latin lateralis ‘of the side’ + rectus ‘straight’. So it means ‘the outer straight muscle’ of the eye.
origin: Common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn)
insertion: Lateral sclera, anterior to the equator of the eyeball
tip: ‘LR6’: abducens abducts — a CN VI palsy means the eye cannot look outward (horizontal double vision).

name: Superior oblique
etymology: From Latin superior ‘upper’ + obliquus ‘slanting’. So it means ‘the upper slanting muscle’ of the eye — its tendon runs obliquely back after hooking through the trochlea.
origin: Body of sphenoid, superomedial to the optic canal
insertion: Sclera, posterosuperolateral quadrant (tendon passes through the trochlea)
tip: ‘SO4’: test by looking in (adduct) then down; CN IV palsy causes trouble going down stairs or reading, with a compensatory head tilt.

name: Inferior oblique
etymology: From Latin inferior ‘lower’ + obliquus ‘slanting’. So it means ‘the lower slanting muscle’ of the eye.
origin: Orbital surface of maxilla, anteromedial floor of orbit (lateral to nasolacrimal groove)
insertion: Sclera, posteroinferolateral quadrant (deep to lateral rectus)
tip: Test by looking in (adduct) then up. The only extra-ocular muscle not arising at the back of the orbit.

name: Levator palpebrae superioris
etymology: From Latin levator ‘lifter’ + palpebrae ‘of the eyelid’ (palpebra) + superioris ‘upper’. So it means ‘the lifter of the upper eyelid’.
origin: Lesser wing of sphenoid, above and in front of the optic canal
insertion: Skin and tarsal plate of the upper eyelid (via its aponeurosis)
innervation: Oculomotor nerve (CN III), superior division; smooth superior tarsal part by sympathetics
tip: Ptosis = CN III palsy (complete droop) or Horner’s syndrome (mild droop from the sympathetic superior tarsal muscle).

name: Genioglossus
etymology: From Greek geneion ‘chin’ + glōssa ‘tongue’. So it means ‘the chin-to-tongue muscle’.
origin: Superior mental spine (genial tubercle) of mandible
insertion: Dorsum of tongue and body of hyoid
actions: Depresses the centre of the tongue
Deviates tongue to the opposite side (unilateral)
tip: With a CN XII lesion the protruded tongue deviates TOWARD the weak side; genioglossus also keeps the airway open in sleep.

name: Hyoglossus
etymology: From Greek hyoeidēs ‘U-shaped’ (hyoid) + glōssa ‘tongue’. So it means ‘the hyoid-to-tongue muscle’.
origin: Body and greater horn of hyoid
insertion: Side and inferior surface of the tongue
tip: Landmark in the floor of mouth: lingual nerve and CN XII lie on it, lingual artery runs deep to it.

name: Palatopharyngeus
etymology: From Latin palatum ‘palate, roof of the mouth’ + Greek pharynx ‘throat’. So it means ‘the palate-to-throat muscle’.
origin: Hard palate and palatine aponeurosis
insertion: Lateral pharyngeal wall and posterior border of thyroid cartilage
actions: Elevates pharynx and larynx during swallowing
Draws palatopharyngeal arches together, helping close off the nasopharynx
innervation: Vagus nerve (CN X) via pharyngeal plexus
tip: Forms the palatopharyngeal arch (posterior pillar) behind the palatine tonsil.

name: Superior pharyngeal constrictor
etymology: From Latin superior ‘upper’ + Greek pharynx ‘throat’ + Latin constrictor ‘one that draws tight’ (constringere). So it means ‘the upper throat squeezer’.
origin: Pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, posterior mylohyoid line of mandible, side of tongue
insertion: Pharyngeal tubercle of occipital bone and median pharyngeal raphe
innervation: Vagus nerve (CN X) via pharyngeal plexus
tip: Shares the pterygomandibular raphe with buccinator — the cheek wall is continuous with the pharynx wall.

name: Middle pharyngeal constrictor
etymology: From Latin medius ‘middle’ + Greek pharynx ‘throat’ + Latin constrictor ‘one that draws tight’. So it means ‘the middle throat squeezer’.
origin: Stylohyoid ligament and greater and lesser horns of hyoid
insertion: Median pharyngeal raphe
innervation: Vagus nerve (CN X) via pharyngeal plexus
tip: Fan-shaped from the hyoid — the constrictors overlap like stacked cups, inferior outside middle outside superior.

name: Inferior pharyngeal constrictor
etymology: From Latin inferior ‘lower’ + Greek pharynx ‘throat’ + Latin constrictor ‘one that draws tight’. So it means ‘the lower throat squeezer’.
origin: Oblique line of thyroid cartilage (thyropharyngeus) and side of cricoid cartilage (cricopharyngeus)
insertion: Median pharyngeal raphe; cricopharyngeus encircles the pharyngo-oesophageal junction
actions: Cricopharyngeus acts as the upper oesophageal sphincter
innervation: Vagus nerve (CN X) via pharyngeal plexus, plus external and recurrent laryngeal branches
tip: A weak spot between its two parts (Killian’s dehiscence) is where a Zenker’s diverticulum forms.

name: Stylopharyngeus
etymology: From Greek stylos ‘pillar’ (the styloid process) + pharynx ‘throat’. So it means ‘the styloid-to-throat muscle’.
origin: Medial side of styloid process of temporal bone
insertion: Posterior and superior borders of thyroid cartilage and pharyngeal wall (with palatopharyngeus)
tip: The only muscle supplied by CN IX.

name: Cricothyroid
etymology: From Greek krikos ‘ring’ (cricoid cartilage) + thyreoeidēs ‘shield-shaped’ (thyroid cartilage). So it means ‘the ring-to-shield muscle’ — between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages.
origin: Anterolateral surface of cricoid arch
insertion: Straight part: inferior margin of thyroid lamina; oblique part: inferior horn of thyroid cartilage
actions: Tilts thyroid cartilage forward on cricoid
Lengthens and tenses the vocal folds (raises pitch)
innervation: External laryngeal nerve (branch of superior laryngeal nerve, CN X)
tip: The only intrinsic laryngeal muscle NOT supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve; injury (e.g. thyroid surgery) loses high notes.

name: Posterior crico-arytenoid
etymology: From Greek krikos ‘ring’ (cricoid) + arytaina ‘ladle, pitcher’ + eidos ‘form’ (arytenoid, ladle-shaped) + Latin posterior ‘behind’. So it means ‘the back ring-to-ladle muscle’.
origin: Posterior surface of cricoid lamina
insertion: Muscular process of arytenoid cartilage
actions: Abducts the vocal folds (opens the rima glottidis)
tip: The ONLY abductor of the vocal folds — bilateral loss threatens the airway (‘safety muscle of the larynx’).

name: Lateral crico-arytenoid
etymology: From Greek krikos ‘ring’ (cricoid) + arytaina ‘ladle’ + eidos ‘form’ (arytenoid) + Latin lateralis ‘of the side’. So it means ‘the side ring-to-ladle muscle’.
origin: Arch of cricoid cartilage
insertion: Muscular process of arytenoid cartilage
actions: Adducts the vocal folds (closes the interligamentous rima glottidis)
tip: Direct antagonist of the posterior crico-arytenoid.

name: Transverse arytenoid
etymology: From Latin transversus ‘lying across’ + Greek arytaina ‘ladle’ + eidos ‘form’ (arytenoid). So it means ‘the muscle lying across the ladle-shaped cartilages’.
origin: Posterior surface of one arytenoid cartilage
insertion: Posterior surface of the opposite arytenoid cartilage
actions: Draws the arytenoids together, closing the posterior (intercartilaginous) rima glottidis
tip: The only unpaired intrinsic laryngeal muscle.

name: Oblique arytenoid (aryepiglottic part)
parts: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle
etymology: From Latin obliquus ‘slanting’ + Greek arytaina ‘ladle’ + eidos ‘form’ (arytenoid); aryepiglottic adds epi ‘upon’ + glōttis ‘mouth of the windpipe’. So it means ‘the slanting arytenoid muscle continuing to the epiglottis’.
origin: Muscular process of one arytenoid cartilage
insertion: Apex of the opposite arytenoid, continuing in the aryepiglottic fold to the lateral margin of the epiglottis
actions: Closes the laryngeal inlet (sphincter during swallowing)
Draws the arytenoids together (adducts vocal folds)
tip: The two oblique arytenoids cross in an X behind the transverse arytenoid.

name: Thyro-arytenoid
etymology: From Greek thyreoeidēs ‘shield-shaped’ (thyroid cartilage) + arytaina ‘ladle’ + eidos ‘form’ (arytenoid). So it means ‘the shield-to-ladle muscle’.
origin: Posterior surface of thyroid cartilage near the midline (angle)
insertion: Anterolateral surface and vocal process of arytenoid; thyro-epiglottic fibres to the aryepiglottic fold and epiglottis
actions: Relaxes and shortens the vocal folds (lowers pitch)
Thyro-epiglottic part widens the laryngeal inlet
tip: Its deepest medial fibres form the vocalis, which fine-tunes vocal-fold tension.
